masters.title: Lesion morphology prediction during microwave ablation for cancer
masters.degree: MSc Biomechanical & Biomedical Engineering (M2), École Polytechnique · IP Paris
masters.confidential: Industrial internship: this page shows the ideas and methods; clinical images and simulation outputs stay with Hepta Medical.
masters.eli5: Doctors can cook a tumour from the inside with a tiny microwave needle. The hard part is knowing exactly how big the cooked zone gets. I measured it in experiments and rebuilt it in simulations so the device can predict it.

steps.title: The problem
steps.eli5: Heat doesn't spread the same way in a living body.
steps.text: Microwave ablation destroys tumours with heat from a 2.45 GHz antenna. Ablation size follows the delivered energy closely ex vivo (>90 % prediction accuracy) but drops to 50–70 % in vivo.
more: Blood vessels carry heat away (the heat-sink effect)
Tissue contracts and changes its properties as it heats
Perfusion and tissue type change how the zone grows over time; ablation volume isn't linear in delivered energy

steps.title: Measuring temperature from inside
steps.eli5: The needle also works as a thermometer.
steps.text: Hepta's 17G water-cooled monopole antenna integrates radiometric temperature sensing: the heated tissue's thermal radiation is read back as a volumetric temperature around the antenna.
more: Designed and fabricated a new burn fixture
Validated and calibrated the radiometer in water baths at 25 °C and 50 °C, cooling on and off
Phantom burns at 75 W and 100 W to compare antenna and radiometric temperatures

steps.title: Ex vivo burns
steps.eli5: Practise on tissue first, with fake blood vessels.
steps.text: Three kinds of benchmark burns in ex vivo tissue, measured by dissection and automatic MATLAB volume analysis.
more: Fixture burns submerged at 37 °C at 3, 7 and 11 mm from a channel, to mimic perfusion and heat sinks
Half burns to watch tissue contraction directly
Bulky burns for full-size ablation zones
Ablation zones split into coagulation and congestion volumes and correlated with delivered energy

steps.title: Simulation
steps.eli5: Build the same burn inside a computer.
steps.text: Coupled electromagnetic and Pennes bioheat models, validated in 2D and 3D, then 30 fixture simulations (21 liver, 9 lung) across powers and depths.
more: Stationary EM heating source coupled to transient bioheat (weak coupling)
Heat-sink asymmetry grows with power near vessels; asymmetric 54 °C isotherms at 3 and 7 mm
Liver and lung behave differently: in lung the zone grows along the antenna and plateaus
Simulated radiometric signals and real-time ablation volumes

steps.title: Outcome
steps.eli5: The computer and the real burns agree on the trend.
steps.text: A benchmarked simulation framework supporting Hepta's radiometry-based prediction, with experiment–simulation correlation of maximum tissue temperature and ablation volume.
more: Foundation for preclinical analysis and early patient-specific simulations
Tools: COMSOL Multiphysics, MATLAB, ex vivo experimentation, CT image analysis

auv.title: Black Pearl: an autonomous underwater vehicle
auv.degree: BTech Mechanical Engineering, Mahindra École Centrale (Mahindra University)
auv.role: Deputy team lead & mechanical subdivision lead
auv.eli5: A small robot submarine that swims and makes decisions on its own. We designed it, built it, and took it to an international competition.

steps.title: The brief
steps.eli5: Fit a whole robot sub inside a suitcase-sized box.
steps.text: Design a vehicle within the SAUVC rule book and the team's own targets.
more: Rule book: under 70 × 50 × 50 cm and 40 kg in air
Targets: 65 × 47.5 × 47.5 cm, 20–22 kg, 5 active degrees of freedom (surge, sway, heave, roll, yaw)
Slight positive buoyancy (4 %) and pitch within 0–10°
The report sets the design to favour stability over speed
A complete AUV has three subsystems (mechanical, electrical, intelligence and vision); the project report documents the mechanical one

figures.caption: The finished vehicle, AUV MEC, Mahindra École Centrale.

steps.title: A modified V-cycle
steps.eli5: Test on the computer first, then build.
steps.text: A systems-engineering V-cycle adapted for a student team: virtual prototyping, then a decision matrix, then physical prototyping.
more: Every component and the assembly rated 1–5 on stability & speed, modularity & structural integrity, ease of in-house fabrication, and aesthetics
Threshold of 2.5/5 to move to a physical prototype
5 design iterations and 2 loops back to verification; most changes caught virtually, before pre-qualification

steps.title: Concept and layout
steps.eli5: Pick the body, the number of hulls and where the thrusters point.
steps.text: Four body concepts were compared: torpedo, glider, body on frame and enclosed body. Torpedo and glider were dropped for control and stability and for needing speed to dive; body on frame and enclosed body went forward. Among hull and thruster layouts, two hulls with six thrusters won because everything fits and all degrees of freedom are available.

head: Layout
Verdict
rows: Selected: more control and stability, at the cost of power

more: Horizontal thrusters sit at 45 degrees (thruster vectoring), so the motor polarities give surge, sway and yaw; surge speed is 1.414 times that of a two-thruster layout
Design basis: body on frame, two hulls, six thrusters, thruster vectoring, dynamic buoyancy control
Rotatable servo-driven thrusters were considered and set aside because of watertight connections and the powerful servos they need
Pressure hulls are an acrylic pipe with an IP47-rated O-ring, aluminium end caps, an acrylic dome and electronics trays
Iteration 1: one cylindrical hull, one cuboid hull, acrylic dome, 3D-printed thruster mounts, rectangular beams and side frames

figures.caption: Final design after four iterations, CAD render.

steps.title: Materials and structure
steps.eli5: Strong where it matters, light everywhere else.
steps.text: Stress simulations gave a minimum acrylic hull thickness of 5 mm with a safety factor of 2. Beam and frame thickness were swept from 1 to 10 mm in aluminium, HDPE and nylon: HDPE deformed 10 to 15 times more than aluminium, so aluminium bars were chosen. The report closes with an open frame of T-slotted aluminium extrusion, compared against rectangular beams under the same load.
more: Hulls: acrylic. Side frames and beams: aluminium or HDPE. End caps: aluminium. Thruster mounts and tray mounts: PLA
Open-frame vehicle: 625 × 475 × 475 mm, frame 8 kg, about 18 kg assembled without the manipulator
T-slot profile: 25 × 25 mm, 2.14 mm wall, 5 mm tappable hole for M5 bolts
The 25 mm rectangular beam deforms least but weighs 900 g against 334 g for the extrusion, which also eases mounting

figures.caption: Stress distribution in the acrylic pipe (left) and deflection of the frame and beams (right).
Open-frame concept in T-slotted aluminium extrusion.

steps.title: Hydrodynamics (CFD)
steps.eli5: Test how the water pushes back, before it ever touches water.
steps.text: The vehicle was simplified in ANSYS SpaceClaim, meshed in ANSYS Meshing and solved in ANSYS Fluent. The mesh was refined over four runs until the result stopped changing (final mesh 451,099 nodes, 2,378,057 elements). Drag was computed in surge, sway and heave; added mass came from potential flow, checked against a sphere first.
more: Mesh relative error over the four runs: 11.89 %, 5.63 %, 1.06 %, then the reference
Fluent models: inviscid for added mass, laminar up to 0.46 m/s, realizable k-ε with scalable wall functions above that, steady and transient
Stationary body in moving fluid, velocity inlet and pressure outlet, no-slip walls, residual 1e-6
The quadratic and linear drag coefficients feed Fossen's equations for the control model

figures.caption: Pressure contour on the vehicle in the CFD run.
Surge drag against velocity with its quadratic fit.

steps.title: Stability and buoyancy
steps.eli5: Heavy at the bottom, so it stays upright.
steps.text: A stable vehicle keeps its centre of mass below its centre of buoyancy. The first assembly had the centre of gravity above the centre of buoyancy, so the bottom hull was shortened from 45 cm to 30 cm. The assembly then weighed 98 N against about 200 N of buoyancy, so 5 kg of dead weights were added until the centre of gravity sat below the centre of buoyancy.
more: Dead weights also bring the positive buoyancy down to the target
Final vehicle: 2.91 % positive buoyancy and pitch of 3 to 6 degrees

steps.title: Fabrication and iteration
steps.eli5: We machined most of it ourselves, and fixed what broke.
steps.text: Most parts were made in house on a bench lathe, CNC milling, a CNC lathe and a bench drill. Groove depth and width for the O-rings were found by trial and error. Side frames were CNC milled at 2.5 kg each. Iteration 4 aimed at a more rigid, simpler vehicle.

head: Part
Change in iteration 4
Why
rows: 3D-printed to aluminium with Al angle (4 nuts and bolts to 2)
4 L-clamps to 2 Al angles plus hull stopper
Less drag, space for gripper connector

more: End caps weigh 580.6 g, 542.1 g and 605.6 g for three of the four caps (the fourth weight is not given in the report)
Thruster mounts printed in PLA at 100 % and 20 % infill and strength tested
Connectors: M10 and M14 bolts drilled through, head filled with potting compound, with O-rings
Electronics trays are acrylic with 3D-printed supports
16 fewer nuts and bolts on each frame

figures.caption: Machining the end caps: CNC milling, lathe work and the finished cap with O-ring grooves.
The vehicle after assembly, with 3D-printed thruster mounts.

steps.title: Testing and thermal study
steps.eli5: Make sure nothing leaks and nothing overheats.
steps.text: Hulls were filled with water overnight to check for leaks. For heat, the main heat sources were run at full capacity in an airtight box for one hour, with a thermometer, a DHT22 and an LM35 recording temperatures. A COMSOL conjugate heat-transfer model then checked the electronics: the ESCs fail at 353 K and the simulation peaked at 312 K.
more: Heat sources modelled: Jetson Nano, electronic speed controllers, Li-Po battery and relays
Heat path: conduction, surface radiation, convection in the hull air, then convection and conduction through the aluminium end caps to the water
Two cases: Boussinesq approximation and compressible flow; 120 s at 0.25 s steps
Manual mesh with 2,022,611 tetrahedral elements, finer on the ESCs

figures.caption: Measured temperature of the circuit board, heat-sink fin and far-away air during the full-load heat run.
COMSOL temperature field inside the hull (2D).

steps.title: Gripper, vision and acoustics
steps.eli5: Hands, eyes and ears for the robot.
steps.text: Three grippers were compared: a fibre-reinforced soft gripper, a print-in-place TPU gripper and a servo gripper. The servo gripper won on durability, cost and modularity. A Logitech C270 camera and a Jetson Nano run object detection, and a hydrophone array is the design for locating a pinger.
more: Gripper: eight-finger aluminium claw, 160 mm maximum opening, two MG995 servos; 600 g load at 30 cm reach needs 18 kg-cm, 27 kg-cm with a safety factor of 1.5
Voice-controlled app through an Arduino Uno and HC-05 Bluetooth module
Vision pipeline: grayscale, Gaussian blur, adaptive threshold, morphological opening, Canny edges, contours filtered by area and aspect ratio, centroid offsets in a ROS and OpenCV setup
Gate and buoy detection tested on pool footage with bounding-box and rotated-rectangle methods
Acoustics: hydrophones spaced by half a wavelength for 37.5 kHz and 45 kHz pingers, pre-amplifier, band-pass filter and FFT, then time-difference-of-arrival and delay-sum beamforming

figures.caption: Gate detection on pool footage: original frame and detected gate.

steps.title: The final vehicle
steps.eli5: It came out right on target.
steps.text: 60 × 47 × 37.5 cm, 20.6 kg in air, positive buoyancy of 2.91 %, pitch 3–6°, with all 5 active degrees of freedom.
more: Published at MTS/IEEE OCEANS 2021 (San Diego – Porto)
Project funded by École Centrale School of Engineering, Mahindra University

steps.title: Building the team
steps.text: Four students designed and built the vehicle as the SE 421/SE 422 project, supervised by Dr Sebastian Uppapalli, with fabrication guidance from Dr Abhijit Bhattacharyya. Sai was deputy team lead and mechanical subdivision lead, and founded the club from scratch: 15 associate and 10 junior members, finances, logistics, logo, social media, a TV interview and news coverage.

auv.report: Design and Development of Autonomous Underwater Vehicle, project report for SE 421/SE 422, Mahindra École Centrale, College of Engineering, Hyderabad, May 2020
auv.scope: The project report covers the mechanical subsystem: design iterations and validation, CFD, fabrication, prototyping and testing, plus the gripper, image processing, acoustic localisation and a thermal study of the electronics. The electrical and intelligence subsystems are the other two parts of a complete AUV.
